notes.b: Every physical activity needs agreed limits on what players may do, otherwise nobody could compete on equal terms. Rules are those limits, written down and applied by someone neutral.
points: Rules are the formal, written regulations of an activity, set by its governing body (the organisation in charge of the sport) and enforced by officials such as referees, so every player is judged by the same standard.
Rules cover scoring, permitted actions, the playing area and equipment, and time, so everyone knows what counts as a point, what is allowed, where play happens and how long it lasts.
Rules also set sanctions. A sanction is a penalty for breaking a rule, such as a free kick, a card or a suspension, and it stops players gaining from cheating.
Offside in soccer: an attacker in an offside position when a team-mate plays the ball forward may be penalised, and the defending team is awarded an indirect free kick.
Four-step rule in Gaelic football: a player may take four steps while holding the ball, then must bounce, hand-pass or kick it, so nobody can simply run with the ball.
Foot fault in tennis: a server's foot touches the line, or the court beyond it, before the ball is struck, so the serve is not allowed.
notes.tip: If asked to outline three rules of a named activity, pick rules you are sure of, such as offside, the four-step rule or a foot fault, and say what each one stops or allows. Describe rules generally if unsure of the detail.

notes.b: Not everything around a game is about winning points. Rituals are the repeated, symbolic actions that give a game its sense of occasion.
points: Rituals are customary, often symbolic actions repeated before, during or after an activity. They are repeated traditions that give the activity a sense of occasion.
The national anthem is played before an international match, which reminds players and supporters that they are representing their country.
The haka is performed by the New Zealand men's rugby team before international matches, expressing the team's identity and tradition.
A team huddle before the start focuses the group on a shared goal, so players begin the contest united.
A minute's silence honours a person or event, giving everyone present a moment to show respect together.
notes.tip: When defining a ritual, stress that it is customary and symbolic, then give a named example such as the haka or the anthem.

notes.b: Some good behaviour is expected in sport even though no rule demands it. These unwritten codes are conventions, and they are what keep competition respectful.
points: Conventions are unwritten codes of behaviour that participants are expected to follow, and that the rules do not enforce. Players follow them out of respect, not fear of a penalty.
Shaking hands with opponents and officials after a match shows that the contest is over and respect remains.
Kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured, then returning possession to the opposing team at the restart, puts care for a player ahead of gaining an advantage.
A tennis player raises a hand to apologise for a net cord winner (a point won by luck when the ball clips the net), acknowledging the opponent was unlucky.
Applauding opponents off the field after a hard contest shows respect for their effort.
A convention becomes a rule when the rule-book requires it, such as a rule about kit colours. Once written into the rules it is enforced, so it is no longer a convention.
notes.tip: The common trap is calling something a convention when the rule-book requires it. If it is written and enforced, it is a rule; a convention is always unwritten.

notes.h: Why rules, rituals and conventions matter
notes.b: Each of the three does a different job. Together they make an activity fair, meaningful and respectful.
points: Rules make competition fair and safe, because everyone plays under the same limits and dangerous actions can be punished.
Rituals build identity, tradition and focus, because repeating them binds a team and its supporters together and prepares players mentally.
Conventions express respect and fair play and keep the spirit of the game, because they cover the good behaviour that rules cannot list or enforce.
notes.tip: A question asking you to define rules, rituals and conventions as they relate to physical activity (set at Higher Level) is worth 8 marks, so learn a precise definition of each: rules are written and enforced by officials, rituals are customary and symbolic, and conventions are unwritten and not enforced by the rules.

notes.h: Organising an event that respects them
notes.b: An event only respects the rules, rituals and conventions of an activity if the organiser plans for them. Good organisation has three stages: planning, building in traditions, and evaluating afterwards.
points: Planning: the fixture and format (who plays whom, and how the competition is structured), the venue and the equipment are set in advance so nothing is left to chance on the day.
Officials are appointed and briefed, and the rules are clarified to teams in advance, so everyone applies and expects the same rules.
A scoring and recording system is in place before the first contest, so results are accurate and disputes can be settled.
Roles are assigned to the organiser, officials, timekeeper, first aid and stewards (people who guide spectators and keep order), so everyone knows their job.
Rituals are built in, such as team introductions before the start, which give the event a sense of occasion.
Conventions are built in: handshakes at the end, presentation of awards, and acknowledgement of officials and opponents, which promote respect.
Evaluation checks whether the event ran on time and whether rules were applied consistently.
Evaluation also checks whether participants behaved respectfully and what would change next time, so the next event improves.
notes.tip: Organising questions reward answers that cover planning, rituals and conventions, and evaluation.

notes.h: Respectful communication with players and officials
notes.b: Communication is part of respecting an activity. How you speak to players and officials affects performance, behaviour and the atmosphere of the whole event.
points: With players: give clear, calm instructions and listen before reacting, so players understand what is wanted and feel heard.
With players: use encouragement rather than criticism, and appropriate language, because positive comments keep confidence and effort high.
With officials: accept decisions without dissent, meaning no arguing, gesturing or shouting, because dissent damages the spirit of the game.
With officials: ask questions through the captain at an appropriate time, not by confronting the official during play.
Thank officials after the contest, which shows respect for the job they do.
notes.tip: For communicating with officials, list the four behaviours: accept decisions, no dissent, questions through the captain at an appropriate time, and thanks.

notes.b: Much of what is communicated in sport is not spoken. In a noisy venue, a gesture or a look can reach a player when words cannot.
points: Hand signals, such as a referee's signals, communicate decisions quickly to players and spectators, even from a distance or over crowd noise.
Body language and gestures show approval, instruction or warning without words, so a nod or open posture can reassure a player.
Eye contact holds a player's attention and shows that the message is meant for them.
Tone of voice: a calm, steady tone reduces tension, while a sharp tone signals urgency, so the same words can feel very different.
notes.tip: Non-verbal communication covers body language, eye contact, gestures, hand signals and tone of voice. Name several and say what each achieves.

notes.b: Good communicators in sport share a set of habits that make a message clear and trusted.
points: A clear voice, projected so every team-mate can hear, means instructions are not missed.
Short, precise instructions given at the right moment are easy to act on, while long ones are forgotten or arrive too late.
Active listening means checking understanding by listening carefully and asking questions, so messages are received correctly.
Consistent signals: the same gesture or call always means the same thing, so there is no confusion in the middle of play.
Whistle use: a clear, distinct blast signals a stoppage or a restart, so everyone knows play has changed.
notes.tip: If asked for three effective communication skills other than hand signals, choose from clear voice, short precise instructions, positive body language, active listening, use of a whistle, consistent signals and eye contact, and say why each works.

keyTerms.definition: The formal, written regulations of an activity, set by its governing body and enforced by officials.
Customary, often symbolic actions repeated before, during or after an activity.
Unwritten codes of behaviour that participants are expected to follow but that the rules do not enforce.
The organisation that sets and maintains the rules of an activity.
A penalty given for breaking a rule, such as a free kick, a card or a suspension.
A soccer rule under which an attacker in an offside position when a team-mate plays the ball forward may be penalised.
Playing within the rules and respecting opponents, officials and the spirit of the activity.
A standard gesture an official uses to communicate a decision.
Messages sent through body language, gestures, eye contact and tone of voice rather than words.
Listening carefully and checking understanding by asking questions.
A team member who represents the team with officials and communicates on its behalf.

questions.prompt: Define rules, rituals and conventions as they relate to physical activity, giving an example of each.
questions.model: Rules are the formal, written regulations of an activity, set by its governing body and enforced by officials; for example, the offside rule in soccer penalises an attacker who is in an offside position when a team-mate plays the ball forward. Rituals are customary, often symbolic actions repeated before, during or after an activity; for example, the national anthem is played before an international match. Conventions are unwritten codes of behaviour that participants are expected to follow but that are not enforced by the rules; for example, shaking hands with opponents and officials after a match.

questions.prompt: Outline three effective communication skills a player or coach can use with officials.
questions.model: First, a clear, calm voice: speaking respectfully and at a reasonable volume, so the official can hear a question without any argument. Second, asking questions through the captain at an appropriate time, such as a stoppage, rather than interrupting play. Third, active listening: listening to the official's explanation fully and acknowledging the decision, which shows respect and keeps the contest under control.
